body.text: November saw a slew of summits in South-East Asia and China, and in Manila, India was represented by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The agenda in Manila (November 15-17) included the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit, the 21st East Asia Summit, and, on the sidelines, a Quad Leaders Summit that brought the leaders of Australia, India, Japan, and the US together. India attended all the Manila deliberations.

In Shenzhen, Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting (November 18-19) and the first-of-its-kind US-China-Russia trilateral (US President Donald Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin) surprise summit on the sidelines. India is not an APEC member and did not participate in the Shenzhen meetings.

The summit that elicited the greatest interest and enthusiastic commentary was the trilateral meeting between the US, China, and Russia hosted by Xi. Comparison was made with the 1945 Yalta Summit, and exaggerated analysis preceded the event itself.

The Shenzhen Declaration issued by the three leaders is modest, broad-spectrum, and anodyne, but two elements merit review: the first related to nuclear weapons and the second, a self-serving advisory to global jurisprudence.

The global nuclear domain, which is currently unregulated—with no consensual guardrails—was highlighted at Shenzhen but with no numbers, no timelines, no verification. Yet modesty must be judged against the vacuum it entered. With the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) having lapsed in February and China refusing trilateral talks, there was no global nuclear dialogue table at all.

On November 19, for the first time, the three largest nuclear powers sat at the same table and agreed, in writing, that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and that they would talk about reducing nuclear risks. That is not a breakthrough. It is a slender silver lining—a signal that the door, which had been slammed shut, is now at least ajar. There is a Reagan-Gorbachev echo in Xi’s language that should not be dismissed. “A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” was first uttered by Ronald Reagan in his 1984 State of the Union address, was made a joint US-Soviet statement at Geneva in November 1985, and was then tested to near-breaking point at Reykjavík in October 1986, where Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev came within hours of agreeing to eliminate all nuclear weapons.

Xi revived the phrase in Shenzhen, adding his own flourish: nuclear weapons are a “sword of Damocles” hanging over humanity, and must be comprehensively prohibited and completely destroyed. One caution is necessary here. Xi’s call for “complete elimination” is not a negotiating concession. It is China’s classic maximalist position: demand zero for everyone, knowing the US and Russia, at more than 5,000 warheads each, will never accept it, while China, at an estimated 620 today, adds roughly 100 a year and is projected to cross 1,000 by 2030. Zero is a slogan, not a schedule.

And yet, for the first time, Beijing agreed to sit at the same table as Washington and Moscow and sign its name to a trilateral commitment to dialogue on nuclear risks. Until Shenzhen, China had said it was neither fair nor realistic to join any arms-control framework while it was so far behind. Trump, for his part, had rejected Russia’s plea for a simple New START extension and insisted on a “new, improved, and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. The result was paralysis: no US-Russia treaty, no US-Russia-China treaty, and no dialogue.

Shenzhen does not break that paralysis. At best, as arms-control veterans warned, it could start a process. There is no cap, no freeze, no inspection, and no date for the next meeting. But diplomacy also works by precedent. The precedent now exists: three leaders at one table agreeing to a joint declaration. The next conversation, about hotlines, notifications of missile launches, and fissile material, will be harder to refuse when the leaders have agreed that nuclear war must never be fought.
That is why the slender silver lining deserves to be welcomed, even as we refuse to mistake it for substance.
The ICC clause

The second strand, tucked into the Shenzhen Declaration, is indicative of the texture of the peace the three nuclear powers were actually protecting. Apropos global jurisprudence, it noted gravely: “The three heads of state recognised that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court [ICC] and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
In an incongruous assertion, three major powers—none of them members of the ICC—sat in Shenzhen together to lecture the court on jurisdiction.

Russia is not a member, and Putin has been under an ICC arrest warrant since March 2023 for the deportation of Ukrainian children. The United States is not a member, the Trump administration has sanctioned ICC officials, and its closest ally in West Asia, (soon to be former) Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, faces ICC proceedings over Gaza.

China is not a member, and it has been doubly disparaging about international adjudication, dismissing the 2016 South China Sea arbitration award under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as “a piece of waste paper” and refusing to participate in the proceedings at all.

This was not equitable jurisprudence, but mutual insurance. The three leaders who agreed that nuclear war must never be fought also agreed, in the same document, that their own officials must never be judged. A club of non-members writing themselves immunity, in the name of peace, while simultaneously rejecting the one tribunal that upheld the rules-based order in Asia’s most contested sea, demonstrated geopolitical chutzpah of a high order.
The Manila initiative
The more significant military initiative from the November slew of summits was not in Shenzhen. It was in Manila, and it was substantive in a way Shenzhen was not.

On the sidelines of the ASEAN and East Asia Summits held in Manila, the Quad leaders recommitted, in language Beijing has tried for a decade to dilute, to a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific; to freedom of navigation and overflight; and to opposing any unilateral attempt to change the status quo by force or coercion.

That is not abstract. In the South China Sea, it is a direct rebuke of Beijing’s grey-zone coercion, maritime militia pressure, and the slow militarisation of features. Manila marked a tangible collective step. The Quad leaders welcomed the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration and announced: “In 2027, our respective P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are scheduled to fly in a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making our seas safer.”

That sentence is the most operational initiative the Quad has ever written about itself. Since 2020, India, Japan, Australia, and the United States have exercised together in Malabar, but have carefully avoided calling it a Quad exercise. Manila dropped the fiction. It put the Quad label on a flight of submarine hunters, India’s P-8I, America’s and Australia’s P-8A, Japan’s P-3C, aircraft built to find, track, and share data on submarines.

The geography is the message. From the East China Sea to the Malacca Strait to the Indian Ocean, the same Chinese submarine fleet that sails from Yulin will now be watched by four militaries sharing one picture. This is what operationalisation looks like: not a communiqué about shared values, but a shared maritime domain awareness architecture that can pick up a destroyer, a submarine, or a missile battery.

Add to this the parallel move in Tokyo, where India and Japan are exploring the use of Indian test ranges at Chandipur for Japan’s 1,000-km Type 25 anti-ship missile. Japan, a US ally, cannot fire that missile at full range in its own crowded archipelago. India can offer the Bay of Bengal. That is not a treaty, but it is both investment and trust, the kind of orientation that deepens when Washington is seen to be courting Beijing.

That irony is the link between Shenzhen and Manila. While Xi, Putin, and Trump were writing impunity into jurisprudence, the Quad was writing the opposite principle into its statement: freedom of navigation, opposition to coercion, and respect for international law, including UNCLOS.
One side is operationalising a rules-based order. The other side is operationalising exemption from it.
Strategic stakes for India
For India, the relevance is not academic. It is geographic and technological. First, the maritime surveillance patrol puts India at the centre of the Quad’s operational turn, not at its periphery.

The Indian Ocean is where Chinese submarines are expanding, where undersea cables run, and where India’s own P-8I fleet, now being expanded, is the only Quad asset that can stay on task for long durations without refuelling politics.
A Quad-branded flight in 2027 means Indian data will feed, and be fed by, American, Australian, and Japanese data in real time. That is a qualitative jump from the Malabar naval exercises.

Second, the related strand of the strategic trapeze is the Chandipur proposal, which, if brought to fruition, solves a problem for Japan and creates leverage for India. It embeds India in the deterrence chain for the First Island Chain without India having to sign a mutual defence treaty or host US bases.

This is strategic autonomy in practice: India provides range safety and geography, Japan provides technology to address a shared threat perception, and both gain a credible anti-ship capability that does not depend on the mood in Washington.

Third, the legal strand is a warning. If the three nuclear powers succeed in normalising the idea that state consent overrides international adjudication, the South China Sea award becomes even more unenforceable, since the pressure on smaller South-East Asian states to accept intimidatory maritime belligerence that tramples law and customary practice increases.

India, which has its own maritime disputes and its own interest in UNCLOS as a shield for smaller states, has every reason to keep the Quad’s legal language alive, even as it keeps its own counsel on the ICC as a non-signatory to the Rome Statute.

Shenzhen allowed Xi to cast himself as a statesman by invoking global zero with respect to nuclear weapons. Manila reminded him that while he was talking about zero, the four democracies were operationalising their ability to find his submarines, test the missiles meant to sink his ships, and write “free and open Indo-Pacific” into summit communiqués without his veto.

The ICC reference told the world that the price of that trilateral photograph was a self-serving shared understanding: we will talk about not fighting each other, and we will agree not to be judged by anyone else.
Yet the silver lining in Shenzhen is worth welcoming. But it is the sharpening of the Quad in Manila that Beijing will be monitoring in the South China Sea and beyond.

For New Delhi, the task now is to convert that maritime surveillance patrol from a 2027 announcement into a regional architecture, before the symbolism of Shenzhen fades and the operational reality crystallises without India.
The November summits are more multi-layered than meets the eye.
Commodore C. Uday Bhaskar (Retd.) is a security analyst and President of the Society for Policy Studies in New Delhi.
